827.title: Diwan Todar Mal
827.hook: tradition says he bought land for the children's cremation by covering it with gold coins
827.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Diwan Todar Mal at Fatehgarh Sahib, where Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade were cremated, and gather there in winter to honor the children and those who stood by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nawab of Malerkotla, who protested when the Guru's younger sons were sentenced. Your line: he spoke up. Today, the same sorrow, answered with gold.

Sirhind, in winter. The sentence has been carried out. The Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, are dead, and tradition says their grandmother, Mata Gujri, died in the cold tower. Now a family is owed one more thing: a cremation. That takes ground, and the ground around Sirhind belongs to people who are afraid of the governor. Nobody wants to be the one who helped. Then a man of the town with wealth and position steps forward and asks to buy a plot. Tradition says the owner named a price meant to make him leave. Today: Diwan Todar Mal.
screen: `SIRHIND, IN WINTER.` → `NOBODY WANTS TO HELP.` → `A PRICE MEANT TO SEND HIM AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here is the price, as tradition tells it. The owner would sell only as much ground as Todar Mal could cover with gold coins. Some tellings go further: the coins had to stand on their edges, side by side, so the cost would be far higher than coins laid flat. Either way, it was an outrageous demand, and Todar Mal didn't bargain. He brought the gold, covered the ground, and bought it. Mata Gujri and the two boys were cremated there with dignity. Sikhs remember the spot at Fatehgarh Sahib, where a gurdwara now stands, and they gather there in winter to remember the children. Three things here are worth slowing down for. First, who he was. Todar Mal was not a Sikh soldier or a member of the Guru's household. Sikh tradition remembers him as a Hindu of Sirhind, a man with position and wealth to lose, and he risked both. Second, who the gift was for: people who could never repay it, a grandmother and two children who had already died. Third, what the gold bought. Not a monument, not a statement, just enough ground to do what a family is owed. Grief, in this story, becomes something practical. Nobody could undo the sentence. Todar Mal did the one thing still left to do, and he did it at full price. Sikhs remember his name with deep gratitude, as a reminder that the person who stands closest in the hardest hour can be a neighbor with a purse and a conscience.
screen: `THE GROUND, COVERED IN GOLD.` · `NOT A SIKH, AND HE RISKED IT ALL.` · `A GIFT NOBODY COULD REPAY.` · `THE ONE THING STILL LEFT TO DO.` · then, large: `GOLD FOR THE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one cause that serves people who can't pay you back: a food bank, a hospice, a gurdwara's langar, a family on your street going through a loss. Picture the gift you could give, money, time or something you own, and notice the urge to bargain it down. Let the first, larger number stand.
Todar Mal. The man of Sirhind who, tradition says, covered the ground in gold so Mata Gujri and the Guru's youngest sons could be cremated. Today's word.
Your line: gold for the children. Full price, for a last kindness. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: Rai Kalha
828.hook: a Muslim chief who sheltered the Guru and sent a messenger to learn the children's fate
828.tomorrow: Mai Bhago, the woman who led
828.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Rai Kalha of Raikot among the people of other faiths who protected Guru Gobind Singh, and his story is told when Sikhs recall the events after Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the younger Sahibzade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwan Todar Mal covered the ground in gold for a cremation. Your line: gold for the children. Today, the Guru himself, and the man who took him in.

A door, and a knock, and a choice. On the other side of the door is Guru Gobind Singh, wanted by the empire. He has come through Chamkaur and Machhiwara, through the forest and the cold, and he doesn't yet know what has happened to his two youngest sons and his mother. On this side of the door is a local chief of Raikot. He's Muslim. He has lands, a family and a lot to lose. Taking the Guru in means taking a risk with all of it. Today: Rai Kalha.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `THE GURU, WANTED BY THE EMPIRE.` → `A CHIEF WITH EVERYTHING TO LOSE.`

segments.voice: Rai Kalha opened the door. Tradition says he welcomed Guru Gobind Singh with respect and kept him under his roof, knowing what it could cost. That's the first thing to hold on to: shelter, given to someone hunted, by a man of another faith. Then he did a second thing, quieter and harder. The Guru wanted news of his family. Sirhind was dangerous ground, so Rai Kalha sent one of his own men, a messenger tradition names Noora Mahi, to find out. Riding into the governor's city, asking questions about the Guru's children, then riding back with whatever he learned. And what he learned was the worst news there is. He told the Guru what had happened at Sirhind: the boys executed, Mata Gujri gone. So Rai Kalha's house is where the Guru heard it. Shelter isn't only a roof. Sometimes it's a place safe enough to hear terrible news. Tradition remembers the parting too. Before he moved on, the Guru gave Rai Kalha a gift in thanks, a vessel his family kept and honored. Sikhs still speak of Rai Kalha with gratitude, alongside the others who stood near the Guru in those weeks: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Todar Mal. In Gurbani, sharan, shelter or refuge, is used for taking refuge in God, and Sikhs speak of coming to the Guru's sharan. In this story, for a few days, the Guru came to someone else's, and was received.

segments.voice: Picture your own door, the real one, and ask who might be knocking on it this week: a friend whose news is bad, a relative who doesn't feel welcome anywhere. Think of one form of shelter you could offer, a seat at your table, a phone you'll pick up, a place to hear hard news without being alone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

Your line: he gave shelter. A roof, and a safe place to hear the worst. Until tomorrow.

829.title: Mai Bhago, the woman who led
829.hook: she shamed the deserters and led them back to fight, and later served as the Guru's guard
829.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mai Bhago and the Muktas at Sri Muktsar Sahib, where the Guru tore up the bedava, and her story is told as an example of courage and of bringing people back to the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rai Kalha of Raikot opened his door to the hunted Guru. Your line: he gave shelter. Today, a woman who went out through her own door and brought people home.

You are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. That, in effect, is what the paper said. During the long siege of Anandpur, tradition says, a band of Sikhs from the Majha country reached the end of what they could bear. Hungry and worn down, they asked to go home. The Guru let them, on one condition: that they put it in writing. Sikhs remember the paper as the bedava, the disclaimer. They signed it and left. Back home in Majha, the news got around, and one woman in the region heard it and would not let it stand. Today: Mai Bhago.
screen: `THE LONG SIEGE OF ANANDPUR.` → `A SIGNED PAPER: NOT OUR GURU.` → `ONE WOMAN WON'T LET IT STAND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Mai Bhago went to the men who had come home and shamed them. Not with a lecture about loyalty, but with a challenge: if they wouldn't stand by the Guru, she would go herself. Some tellings say she offered them women's clothes: they could stay at home, and she would go in their place. It stung, and it worked. The men gathered again, and she rode out at their head to find the Guru. They found him, or rather they found his pursuers. Near a pool of water at Khidrana, the band led by Mai Bhago met the imperial force that was chasing Guru Gobind Singh, and they fought. Tradition says the men fell, and Mai Bhago was wounded. Then comes the part Sikhs tell tenderly. The Guru went among the fallen. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still alive. The Guru held his head in his lap and asked what he wished for. Mahan Singh asked him to tear up the paper. And tradition says the Guru took out the bedava and tore it up. The men who had signed themselves away were his Sikhs again. Sikhs call them the Muktas, the liberated ones, and the place became Muktsar. Mai Bhago didn't go home. Tradition says she stayed near the Guru, served as one of his guards, and traveled south with him to Nanded. But the heart of it is what she did at the start. She didn't write the deserters off. She went to them and led them back.

830.title: Bhai Mani Singh at Damdama
830.hook: the scribe who wrote out the Granth as the Guru dictated, later granthi at the Harmandir
830.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Takht Sri Damdama Sahib at Talwandi Sabo as the place where, tradition says, the Granth was written out with Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns included, and they remember Bhai Mani Singh as scribe, granthi and martyr.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mai Bhago went to the men who had signed away the Guru and led them back. Your line: she led them back. Today, after the battles, a quiet room and a pen.

After Muktsar, the Guru keeps moving, and tradition says he comes to rest at Talwandi Sabo, in the dry Malwa country. Sikhs know the place as Damdama Sahib. For a while there is no siege, no pursuit. And the Guru turns to something that has nothing to do with swords. He begins to recite. Beside him sits a man with ink, a reed pen and a great stack of paper, writing down every line, carefully, as it comes. Today: Damdama Sahib.
screen: `AFTER THE BATTLES, A REST.` → `THE GURU RECITES.` → `A MAN WITH A REED PEN.`

segments.voice: Here is what Sikh tradition says happened at Damdama. Guru Gobind Singh recited the scripture, the Granth that Guru Arjan had compiled, and Bhai Mani Singh wrote it out as he dictated. Into this version, tradition says, the Guru added the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Sikhs remember this as the version of the Granth that the Guru later named as Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib. So look at what Bhai Mani Singh was doing. Not composing. Not editing to his taste. Listening, and writing exactly what he heard, line after line, day after day, without letting his own voice creep in. A scribe's whole skill is to stay out of the way. A careless hand can drop a word. A proud hand can improve one. His job was to do neither. He had been near the Guru's household since boyhood, tradition says, and he stayed close for the rest of his life. Later, tradition says, he was sent to Amritsar to serve as granthi at the Harmandir, the reader and keeper of the scripture there, at a hard and dangerous time for Sikhs. Tradition says that years later, after a dispute with the Lahore authorities over a Diwali gathering of Sikhs at Amritsar, he was executed in Lahore, refusing to give up his faith to save his life, and he is remembered as a martyr. But today belongs to the quieter years: the room at Damdama, the voice reciting, the pen moving. Sikhs sometimes call Damdama the Guru's Kashi, a place of learning. In this telling, its learning starts with someone writing slowly and well.

segments.voice: Find a pen and paper and choose one line that matters to you: a line of Gurbani if you know one, like Ik Onkar, or a line from someone you love. Write it out slowly, every letter, without improving or rushing it; when your mind wanders, return to the next letter. Then read it back once, exactly as written.
Damdama Sahib, Talwandi Sabo in the dry Malwa country, where Guru Gobind Singh recited the Granth and a scribe wrote down every line.
Your line: the steady scribe. Every letter, written exactly as it came. See you tomorrow.

831.title: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh
831.hook: the man who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head was embraced by the tenth Guru, who called his people the Guru's own sons
831.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Jaita, later Bhai Jivan Singh, at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi and at Anandpur, and the young Guru's words 'Rangrete Guru ke bete' are repeated as a sign that the Guru made the overlooked his own family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Mani Singh wrote out the Granth at Damdama Sahib as the Guru recited. Your line: the steady scribe. Today, we step back to an earlier, darker night.

Delhi, in the square of Chandni Chowk. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has just been executed on the emperor's order. His body lies where it fell, with guards around it, as a warning. Sikhs in the crowd are afraid even to be recognized. Then night comes, and with it, in the story, a storm and confusion. And one man moves toward the Guru's body when everyone else is moving away. He is a Sikh named Jaita. Today: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh.
screen: `CHANDNI CHOWK, AFTER THE EXECUTION.` → `GUARDS, AND A CROWD AFRAID.` → `ONE MAN MOVES TOWARD THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bhai Jaita took the Guru's head, wrapped it, and carried it away from Delhi, traveling hard and in secret, all the way to Kiratpur and Anandpur, to the Guru's young son, Gobind Rai. Others took care of the body, and a Sikh named Lakhi Shah burned his own house to cremate it unseen. But it was Jaita who arrived before the boy with his father's head. Here is the moment Sikhs remember. Jaita came from a community that the society around him counted low. The young Guru did not see that. Tradition says he embraced Jaita and said words Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. Not servants. Not followers allowed in at the edge. Sons. A whole people, looked down on by the society around them, named family in one sentence, because one of them had walked toward the Guru's body when others walked away. Years later, when the Khalsa was formed, tradition says Jaita took amrit and received a new name: Jivan Singh. Jivan means life. He became a commander and a poet in the Guru's service, and tradition says he fell at Chamkaur. So his story carries two names. Jaita, the man who carried a head through the night. Jivan Singh, the man the Khalsa made. Between them is the embrace: a boy whose father had just been killed, holding the man who brought him home, and making sure everyone heard what the Guru thought of him.

Your line: the guru's own sons. Two names, and one embrace between them. That's day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: Women of the early Khalsa
832.hook: women took amrit from the start and fought, served, taught and led
832.howItsDone: Sikh women take the name Kaur, as Sikh men take Singh, and the Sikh code of conduct gives it at amrit; Sikhs remember Mata Sahib Kaur, Mai Bhago and Mata Sundari among the women of the early Khalsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Jaita carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head through the night and was embraced as family. Your line: the guru's own sons. Today, the Guru's daughters.

A sign-in sheet at a gurdwara, a class list, a wedding card. Read down the names and a pattern shows up. Harpreet Kaur. Jasleen Kaur. Manjit Kaur. Different first names, the same second one, again and again, where another family's surname might be. It isn't a family name at all. It's a name given by faith, carried by Sikh women whether their families came from one village or from across the world. Where did it come from, and what was it meant to say? Today's word: Kaur.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES.` → `THE SAME SECOND NAME.` → `NOT A FAMILY NAME.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition ties the name to the Khalsa. Men who took amrit were given the name Singh, lion. Women were given Kaur, a name Sikhs explain as princess. As Sikhs tell it, the effect was the same for both: an old surname that announced caste and clan was set aside, and the Khalsa shared a family name instead. A princess answers to no one's idea of where she belongs. Tradition places women in this from the start. The tellings of the first amrit put a woman's hand in the bowl, whether they name Mata Jito or Mata Sahib Kaur, whom Sikhs call the mother of the Khalsa. In the tellings, women took amrit and kept the Khalsa's discipline alongside men. Then look at what they did. Some fought: Mai Bhago, whom we met this week, led the deserters back and later served as the Guru's guard. Some led: Mata Sundari, after Guru Gobind Singh, guided the Sikhs through letters and counsel. Some served and taught, keeping kitchens, raising children in the faith, reciting Gurbani in homes that had no granthi nearby. Sikhs often quote a line of Guru Nanak's here, from Asa di Var in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase, it asks why woman should be called lesser, when from her kings are born. So, as Sikhs explain it, Kaur isn't a decoration but a statement: a woman who signs it signs as royalty, as family, and as a full member of the Khalsa.
screen: `SINGH FOR MEN, KAUR FOR WOMEN.` · `NO CASTE IN THE NAME.` · `THEY FOUGHT, LED, SERVED AND TAUGHT.` · `FROM HER, KINGS ARE BORN.` · then, large: `KAUR MEANS PRINCESS.`

833.title: The Gurus' Muslim friends
833.hook: Mardana, Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi and Ghani Khan: the story is full of them
833.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mardana, Mian Mir, Pir Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla and Rai Kalha with gratitude, and Sheikh Farid's verses are read in the Guru Granth Sahib alongside the Gurus' hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the women of the early Khalsa, and the name they carry. Your line: kaur means princess. Today, the end of the week, and a roll call.

Mardana. Mian Mir. Budhu Shah. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan. Sher Muhammad Khan of Malerkotla. Rai Kalha of Raikot. Say those names one after another, and something becomes hard to miss. From the first Guru's travels to the tenth Guru's darkest winter, again and again at the turning points of the Sikh story, there's a Muslim friend standing close. Playing the music. Laying a foundation. Sending sons into battle. Carrying the Guru in disguise. Speaking up in court. Opening a door. Today: the Gurus' Muslim friends.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF NAMES.` → `AT THE TURNING POINTS.` → `A MUSLIM FRIEND STANDING CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning. Mardana, a Muslim musician from Guru Nanak's own village, traveled with him and played the rebab while the Guru sang. Sikh tradition pictures Guru Nanak's hymns reaching people through the two of them together, the song and the strings. Then Mian Mir, the Sufi of Lahore and a friend of Guru Arjan. Tradition credits Mian Mir with laying the foundation stone of the Harmandir. Then Pir Budhu Shah, who sent his sons and followers to fight beside Guru Gobind Singh at Bhangani, where, tradition says, his sons fell. Then the dark winter after Chamkaur: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan carrying the Guru through enemy lines as a holy man, the Nawab of Malerkotla protesting the sentence on the Guru's youngest sons, and Rai Kalha sheltering the Guru and sending for news. And there's a friendship older than any of them, inside the scripture itself. The Guru Granth Sahib holds verses of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet, beside the hymns of the Gurus. The Sikh story has real enemies in it: an empire's cruelty, a governor's sentence. But in the way Sikhs tell it, that cruelty never becomes a line drawn around a whole faith, because the friends keep turning up on the Guru's side of it. Look back at this week, too. Todar Mal paid gold for the children's cremation. Rai Kalha gave shelter. Mai Bhago led the deserters back. Bhai Mani Singh wrote steadily at Damdama. Bhai Jaita carried the head and was called a son. And the women of the Khalsa took a name that meant they belonged. The Gurus' circle kept widening.
